title: New Grub Street: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: The Grub Street Trap: Setting the Scene

utterances.text: Welcome to New Grub Street Unpacked, the show that takes George Gissing's great novel about literary ambition and failure and asks what it still has to say to us.
New Grub Street, published in 1891, is a novel about writers — writers who succeed, writers who are crushed, and the grinding commercial machinery that determines which is which.
It's a novel about money and art and what happens when they collide — and it is, in my view, one of the most painfully honest books in the English language.
Joining me today to unpack it are three readers who bring very different things to this table.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has voiced more classic novel audiobooks than perhaps anyone alive — he comes to Gissing as a performer who hears the prose from the inside.

Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don whose lifelong conviction is that great novels are above all stories about individual character tested by circumstance — about moral fibre, not social programme.
And Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every novel as an anatomy of class power — and who I suspect will find Gissing exceptionally well-stocked material.
Let's begin with the world Gissing puts us in — this London literary world of the 1880s, the world of Grub Street.
Oliver, you've lived inside a great many novels — how does this one feel different from the first page?
The first thing you notice is the cold.
Not cold as in emotional distance — though that's there too — but the physical, domestic cold of people who cannot afford to be warm.
Gissing is extraordinarily precise about the texture of poverty — the specific indignity of it.
And yet the novel has this extraordinary comedic energy running beneath the tragedy — these wonderfully drawn grotesques, these magnificent operators like Jasper Milvain.
Gissing is ferocious about the literary marketplace, but he's also enormously funny about it — and that combination is what makes the novel a pleasure rather than a punishment.
What strikes me about Reardon and Biffen — the two writers at the heart of the novel — is that Gissing gives them a tenderness and a dignity that the world they inhabit simply refuses to acknowledge.
Oliver is quite right about the texture — Gissing is a novelist of surfaces in the very best sense.
But I would resist the temptation to read this as primarily a novel about a system — an economic mechanism grinding down its victims.
What Gissing is actually exploring — with great psychological subtlety — is why certain men fail and others succeed, and whether the difference lies in will or in circumstance.
Reardon is a fascinating study in a particular kind of moral paralysis — a man of genuine gifts who is undone by his own temperament as much as by his poverty.
Gissing doesn't let his characters off the hook simply because they are poor — and that, I think, is the mark of a genuinely serious novelist.
Edmund raises a real question — about will and circumstance — and I want to press on it, because I think the novel does too.
There's a passage where Reardon himself makes this diagnosis about London — about what the city actually does to men who come to it with ambitions.
"London is only a huge shop, with an hotel on the upper storeys."
That is Reardon speaking — a man who has been broken by the place — and the bitterness of it is earned.
He goes on to say that he thought, as so many men do, that London was still the one centre of intellectual life — and that this belief was the delusion that ruined him.
Now Edmund might say that is a failure of individual judgment — and it is, in part.
But Gissing is showing us that the delusion is structural — it is what the literary marketplace requires of ambitious men in order to feed on them.
"A huge shop, with an hotel on the upper storeys" — I mean, that's a writer at the height of his powers.
The comic cruelty of putting a hotel above a shop — the suggestion that the cultural life London promises is just a bit of gilding over a commercial transaction.
And what I love is that Gissing puts it in the mouth of a character — it's not a narratorial pronouncement, it's a man talking to his friend in extremity.
That's how you write a polemical novel and still write a human one — you earn the ideas through the suffering of real people.
I'll grant that Reardon's diagnosis of London is brilliantly expressed — Gissing rarely wastes a sentence when he is at his best.
But I notice Reardon says 'my mistake' — he owns it as a personal failure of judgment, not as the operation of an impersonal machine.
There is something almost Johnsonian about that — the refusal of self-pity, the turning of the analysis inward.
The question Gissing leaves open — and it is to his great credit that he does — is whether that self-knowledge saves Reardon or merely compounds the tragedy.
And the novel gives us another portrait alongside Reardon's self-diagnosis — Harold Biffen, who suffers just as completely but chooses a different kind of integrity.
There's a moment that I find almost unbearable in its quiet dignity — Biffen describing a consumptive student who came to him for Latin lessons.
"After a lesson or two I told him his cough was too bad, and he had no right to study until he got into better health; that was better, I think, than saying plainly he had no chance on earth."
And then Biffen adds — and this is the line that breaks you — "the food I bought with his money was choking me."
Here is a man who is himself on the edge of starvation, refusing payment out of a scruple so fine that most people in comfort would never even feel it.
That is not merely character — that is the novel showing us what the system costs, in human terms, when the people it grinds are people of genuine moral beauty.
"The food I bought with his money was choking me" — that is one of the great sentences in Victorian fiction, and I will fight anyone who disagrees.
The physicality of it — the food, the choking — it's not metaphor, it's visceral moral experience rendered in the most direct possible English.
And delivered so quietly — no capitals, no exclamation — just a man reporting his own condition to a friend over what I imagine is a very meagre supper.
And that tension — between private moral excellence and public economic annihilation — is precisely where Gissing is most devastating.
In our next segment we turn to the figure at the centre of that devastation — Edwin Reardon himself, and the slow, terrible unraveling of his ambition and his marriage.
We've been mapping the pressures that Grub Street exerts on everyone who enters it.
Now let's put the novel's central figure under the glass — Edwin Reardon, and the question of whether his ruin is tragedy or self-inflicted defeat.
What strikes me first, every time I come back to Reardon, is the sheer physical comedy of his situation — which Gissing absolutely refuses to let be merely comic.
Take the writing of that final volume.
"The last volume was written in fourteen days. In this achievement Reardon rose almost to heroic pitch, for he had much to contend with beyond the mere labour of composition."
And then Gissing proceeds to list what he had to contend with — lumbago, headaches, sore throat, the pawnbroker.
It reads almost like a comic inventory — except it absolutely isn't, because every item on the list is a small humiliation.
And then he finishes, writes 'The End,' and simply — lies back and lets time pass in blankness for a quarter of an hour.
Oliver's right that there's something almost farcical about it — but I want to hold onto what that list actually represents.
Reardon is pawning his watch and selling his books not to live — but to buy himself the time to produce a commodity that may not sell.
And the books he sells — Gissing is very specific about what they are.
"Of course he had chosen from among the most valuable he possessed; such a multitude must else have been sold to make this sum of two pounds ten. Books are cheap, you know."
That sardonic aside — 'Books are cheap, you know' — is Gissing speaking directly to the market that has destroyed his character.
The intellectual labour that produced those books, the years of a poor student's accumulation — rendered worthless by the logic of the trade.
Daniel makes a compelling economic case, and I don't entirely resist it.
But notice what Gissing does at the end of that same passage.
Reardon looks at the gaps on his shelves, mourns his lost books — and then Amy glances at him with sympathy, and he breaks into a cheerful laugh.
The novel insists that love is not reducible to economic pressure.
There is something he values more than the library of his intellectual life — and Gissing honours that, quietly, in one line.
The tragedy, when it comes, is that this love proves insufficient against the grinding pressure of circumstance — not because love was false, but because circumstance is merciless.
And Gissing crystallises that mercilessness in two words — 'A doleful Christmas.'

"A doleful Christmas. Week after week went by and Reardon knew that Amy must have exhausted the money he had given her. But she made no more demands upon him, and necessaries were paid for in the usual way."
'Necessaries were paid for in the usual way' — do you hear the terrible dignity in that phrase?
It's the language of household accounts used to describe a marriage that is quietly coming apart.
And then — 'He suffered from a sense of humiliation; sometimes he found it difficult to look in his wife's face.'
Gissing doesn't explain the psychology — he simply places Reardon before Amy's gaze and says: he cannot meet it.
What I find remarkable is that Gissing shows us the shame without in any way suggesting Reardon deserves it.
The humiliation isn't a moral verdict — it's what the system produces in a man who cannot commodify his talent on demand.
And when Reardon is pressed — when someone asks him what he intends to do — all he can say is this.
"I wish to Heaven I knew!"
Three words of genuine anguish — and notice there's no irony, no self-pity, no performance of despair.
Just the honest admission that he has no plan, no exit, no alternative — and that this helplessness is not weakness of character but the shape of his situation.
I want to enter a mild dissent here, because I think Gissing is more interested in character than Daniel allows.
Consider how Reardon and Biffen first meet — and what that meeting reveals about the man.
Biffen walks into a circulating library and asks for Reardon's books.
"A voice near at hand asked the attendant if he had anything 'by Edwin Reardon.' The novelist turned in astonishment; that any casual mortal should inquire for his books seemed incredible."
'Any casual mortal' — that is not the self-pity of a victim.
That is a man who has made a private peace with his own obscurity, and can still find it faintly absurd.
The question the novel poses is not only what the market does to Reardon — it is what Reardon does, or fails to do, in response.
Edmund, I think you've put your finger on the thing that makes Reardon so genuinely moving rather than merely pitiable.
He retains, for a long time, a quality of rueful self-awareness — he knows exactly how absurd his position is, and that knowledge doesn't save him.
And there's something in the friendship with Biffen that shelters that quality — two men who share the joke of their own irrelevance.
An abusive review had drawn Biffen to Reardon's name — not a glowing notice in a fashionable journal, but a hostile one.
Even their friendship is born under the sign of failure — and Gissing makes that tender rather than grim.
Reardon can see his own ruin with some clarity — and yet cannot escape it.
Which makes the contrast with Jasper Milvain all the more devastating — because Milvain sees the same landscape and makes entirely different choices.
That's where we're headed next — the art of ruthlessness, and what it costs to succeed by Grub Street's rules.

segments.title: The Art of Ruthlessness: Milvain's Calculated Ascent

utterances.text: We've been sitting with Reardon's paralysis — his inability to write, to earn, to hold his marriage together.
Now I want to turn to the figure who seems to move through that same world with almost obscene ease: Jasper Milvain.
Milvain is one of the great comic monsters of Victorian fiction, and I mean that as the highest possible compliment.
He's not a villain who dissembles — he never pretends to be anything other than what he is.
He announces his cynicism with the cheerfulness of a man reading out a train timetable.
And Gissing gives him a perfect comic foil in Whelpdale — the man who fails at everything and then makes a living advising others how to succeed.
Milvain can barely contain himself when he reports it.
"A man who can't get anyone to publish his own books makes a living by telling other people how to write!"
The exclamation mark is doing enormous work there — that's a man who recognises a kindred spirit.
I think we risk making Milvain too comfortable a figure if we treat him purely as a satirical creation.
Gissing is asking something harder than whether the literary market is corrupt.
He's asking whether a man of genuine intelligence who abandons principle is in any meaningful sense still a whole man.
Milvain's clarity about Whelpdale's racket is the clarity of someone who has already made the same bargain, just more elegantly.
The joke lands — Oliver is quite right — but there's a chill underneath it.
That chill is structural, not merely moral.
What Milvain understands — and what Reardon cannot bring himself to accept — is that the literary market doesn't reward talent.
It rewards the appearance of productivity, the performance of relevance, the management of connections.
Whelpdale's advisory scheme isn't a joke — it's a logical extension of how the whole system operates.
And Whelpdale later gives us the most nakedly honest account of what that market actually wants.
"What they want is the lightest and frothiest of chit-chatty information — bits of stories, bits of description, bits of scandal, bits of jokes, bits of statistics, bits of foolery."
That isn't satire — that's a business plan that would feel quite at home today.
The rhythm of that list is extraordinary — Gissing is actually performing the thing he's describing.
Bits, bits, bits — the sentence fragments itself into exactly the kind of chit-chat it's mocking.
It's a formal joke with a very serious point, and only a novelist of real craft could pull it off.
But what interests me equally is what this tells us about Milvain's position.
He doesn't produce this content — he circulates above it, managing the market rather than serving it.
And yet Milvain's ascent carries a cost that I think Gissing traces with great precision.
Consider his treatment of Marian Yule.
Alfred Yule understands Milvain's interest in his daughter with the cold clarity of a man who has spent his life being used by the literary world.
Gissing puts it quite plainly — the suspicion was, as he writes, "rankling in his mind; doubtless it intensified the prejudice which originated in literary animosity."
The father sees the transaction clearly even if the daughter refuses to.
That is, for me, a moral failure of a very particular kind — not wickedness, exactly, but the slow erosion of a man's capacity to value another person for herself alone.
I wouldn't frame it as moral failure — I'd call it the system producing its inevitable outcome.
Milvain has fully internalised the logic of the market: every relationship is an investment, every connection a potential return.
But Marian sees through it — and her response is one of the most devastating moments in the novel.
"I know now how foolish it is when they talk of love being unselfish.
In what can there be more selfishness? I feel as if I could hold you to your promise at any cost.
You don't love me, Jasper, and that's an end of everything."
That is not self-pity — it's a woman performing a precise ethical audit of her own desire and then acting on the result.
What strikes me in that speech is the rhythm of the thinking — it's not elegiac, it's almost forensic.
She's not weeping; she's reaching a conclusion.
And it throws Milvain's whole performance into relief — because next to her precision, his calculations look rather shabby.
He gets what he wants in the novel — the career, the connections, eventually the right marriage.
But Gissing makes sure we've seen the cost of that success in human terms, and it's not negligible.
One might set Milvain's success against what we've just been discussing of Reardon — the man who could not make that bargain.
Gissing gives us Reardon lying awake in the small hours, tormented not only by failure but by the proximate warmth of his wife — the very tenderness he fears to lose.
"The soft breathing of Amy at his side, the contact of her warm limbs, often filled him with intolerable dread."
That is a man destroyed not by cruelty but by the prospect of disappointment — by the gap between what love requires and what he can provide.
Milvain never permits himself such vulnerability — and whether that makes him admirable or diminished is the question Gissing leaves entirely open.
The question Gissing leaves open — and that we've been circling — is who pays the price when the market wins.
Milvain rises; Marian is left to make impossible choices — about love, money, and what a woman of intelligence can actually do in this world.

segments.title: Marian's Impossible Choices: Gender, Labour, and Constraint

utterances.text: We've been watching Jasper Milvain climb — calculating, charming, entirely unimpeded by scruple.
Now I want to turn to someone for whom the literary world offers no such freedom of movement: Marian Yule.
Marian is one of those characters Gissing draws with a kind of aching precision.
She is intelligent, she is capable, she is — and this is the cruelty of it — entirely aware of her situation.
She works in the British Museum Reading Room alongside her father, doing the labour that will make his reputation, not hers.
And when she finally finds something that might be hers — Jasper, the possibility of love — her father becomes the instrument of its destruction.
There's a passage I keep returning to, where Gissing shows us the exact moment Marian nearly breaks.
"She saw her father in his worst aspect, and her heart was shaken by an unnatural revolt from him."
That word — unnatural — is doing so much work.
It's not just revolt. It's revolt that she herself experiences as a transgression against the natural order of things.
Oliver is right to fix on that word, and I think it speaks to something Gissing understands with exceptional clarity about filial feeling.
Marian does not simply rebel. She is horrified by her own rebellion.
And what prompts it is not merely paternal interference but something Gissing names precisely — spite.
The passage continues — and this is the moral centre of it, I think — Gissing writes that a father actuated by simple motives of affection would never speak and look thus.
"A father actuated by simple motives of affection would never speak and look thus."
That is the test Gissing sets. Not convention, not duty — affection.
Alfred Yule fails it absolutely. And Marian, clear-eyed as she is, cannot quite forgive herself for seeing it.
I want to press on something Edmund has opened up, because I think the question of Alfred Yule's motives is inseparable from his economic situation.
Yule is a man whose literary career has failed. His reputation is fading. And Marian's inheritance — the money from her uncle — is the one asset that might still rescue him.
If she marries Jasper Milvain, that capital is gone. That's the hidden engine of his spite.
And Gissing is unsentimental about this. The family itself — the father-daughter relation — becomes a form of labour extraction.
Marian's work in the Reading Room, her intellectual effort, her emotional energy — all of it flows upward to Alfred.
Her revolt is not just filial ingratitude. It is the moment a worker begins to see the structure she has been sustaining.
Daniel, that's brilliantly put — and it makes Jasper's treatment of Marian all the more interesting, doesn't it?
Because Jasper, whatever his faults — and they are considerable and entertaining — actually sees her.
There's a marvellous little exchange where he tells her precisely who she is, in that way he has of flattering by being accurate.
"Dull, by no means. But sage and sober and reticent — and exactly what I like in my friend, because it contrasts with my own habits."
"All the better that merriment lies below it."
Now, that is a man who has paid attention.
Whether it's genuine feeling or performed perception — with Jasper one is never quite sure — the effect on Marian must have been intoxicating.
One must be careful, though, not to make Marian purely a victim of circumstances, however real those circumstances are.
The passage Oliver quoted earlier shows us someone who chooses not to speak. She could trust herself to converse longer — Gissing tells us precisely that she could not.
She restrains herself because the words she might say would change the current of her whole life. That is moral agency, operating under pressure.
And it reminds me, in a minor key, of Reardon's own collapse — that passage where exhaustion becomes something almost gothic.
Gissing writes of Reardon: "At times he was on the border-land of imbecility; his mind looked into a cloudy chaos, a shapeless whirl of nothings."
Reardon's constraint is partly external — poverty, the market — but it is also a failure of will, a slow dissolution of the self from within.
Marian does not dissolve. She endures. And I think that distinction matters enormously.
Edmund, I take the point about Marian's self-restraint — but I'd ask: what are the conditions under which that restraint operates?
She cannot speak freely because to do so would rupture the domestic arrangement on which she is materially dependent.
Agency exercised under that kind of constraint is real — I don't deny it — but we should name what produces the constraint.
And then there is Reardon — the comparison Edmund draws is instructive, and a little devastating.
Reardon talks aloud in the street, not knowing he does so — little fragments of his unfinished work escaping him publicly.
"'What could I make of that, now?' 'Well, suppose I made him—?' 'But no, that wouldn't do.'"
A man publicly dismantling before an indifferent city. That is what the market does to those who cannot perform its rituals with Milvain's facility.
And Marian is watching this — the failure of one man, the studied success of another — and being given no good options between them.
I can't leave Reardon's street-muttering without noting that Gissing has, in fact, given that moment a kind of bleak comedy.
Gissing tells us someone passing catches his eye — "so young a man to be talking to himself in evident distress."
The observer's thought is the sting. So young. As if age would have made it more acceptable.
Gissing is drawing on the same vein of comedy he uses with poor Whelpdale — that sublime mixture of the farcical and the genuinely painful.
Whelpdale opens what he expects to be a love letter and finds that his fiancée has gone back to an old flame in Birmingham.

"She writes — that she has met an old lover — in Birmingham — that it was with him she had quarrelled — not with her father at all — that she ran away to annoy him and frighten him — that she has made it up again, and they're going to be married!"
Every dash is a new blow. Gissing even stages the physical moment — the letter trembling in a pale hand.
Comic, yes — but not unkind. Gissing never quite abandons his characters to pure ridicule.
That balance — the comic and the catastrophic sitting side by side — is something Gissing manages with extraordinary control throughout the novel.
It raises a larger question about how he uses humour — whether the comedy of the literary marketplace is itself a form of critique.
That's where we're headed next — the satire and survival at the heart of New Grub Street's comic vision.

segments.title: Satire and Survival: Comedy in the Literary Marketplace

utterances.text: We've been tracing the weight of constraint on Marian — economic, domestic, psychological.
But Gissing is not only a novelist of suffering — he is also, and this is easy to forget, a satirist of considerable ferocity.
Oliver, you've been waiting to get at the comic texture of this book — and I think this is your moment.
It's a relief, honestly, because there's a comic genius at work in this novel that doesn't always get its due.
People read New Grub Street as a tragedy — and it is — but it's also one of the funniest portraits of the literary world ever written.
Take John Yule — this magnificent philistine who comes thundering in with his denunciations of civilisation.
Gissing gives him this wonderful blunt instrument of a speech — listen to the rhythm of it.
"Your Board schools, your popular press, your spread of education! Machinery for ruining the country, that's what I call it."
That triple hammer-blow at the start — your Board schools, your popular press, your spread of education — it's practically music.
And then the pay-off: machinery for ruining the country.
The joke is that John isn't entirely wrong — Gissing half believes him — which makes it funnier and more unsettling at once.
I think that ambivalence is precisely what gives the satire its edge.
John Yule is a brute, certainly — but he is also a man who has built something, made something with his hands.
And around him Gissing has arranged a cast of literary men who have produced, when you examine them honestly, very little of lasting value.
The satire cuts in multiple directions at once — that is the mark of a serious comic writer.
And yet it's worth noting who John Yule's contempt lands on — not the owners of the press, but the readers.
His complaint is that sedentary workers — the clerks, the counter-hands — are being given access to print culture.
That is the anxiety here: not aesthetic decline, but class mobility through literacy.
Gissing frames it as satire — but the social terror underneath John's bluster is absolutely real.
Daniel's right — though I want to stay with the comedy for a moment longer, because Alfred Yule gives us another specimen entirely.
Where John is a bludgeon, Alfred is a scalpel — a scalpel convinced of its own magnificence.
His critique of literary journalism is genuinely acute — Gissing gives him the best lines.
Listen to this — Alfred holding forth on the state of criticism.
"The evil of the time is the multiplication of ephemerides. Hence a demand for essays, descriptive articles, fragments of criticism, out of all proportion to the supply of even tolerable work."
Ephemerides! He won't say 'periodicals' like a normal person.
And the diagnosis is sound — the market flooding with mediocrity — but then Gissing wheels the camera round.
Alfred descends immediately into a footnote-level dispute about whether 'Epsom Wells' was by Crowne or Shadwell — a question that matters to precisely nobody alive.
The comedy of a man who can diagnose the disease while being a perfect specimen of it — that is Gissing at his most lethal.
It is a particular kind of English comic type — the learned man whose learning has become an affliction.
Dr. Johnson diagnosed it with characteristic economy: 'He that reads and grows no wiser, seldom suspects his own deficiency.'
Alfred Yule has read everything and learned nothing about himself — and that is both the comedy and the pathos of him.
Gissing is not unkind to him — he simply lets Alfred talk, and the portrait paints itself.
What strikes me about Alfred is that his pedantry is inseparable from his economic precarity.
His obsessive fidelity to minor scholarly points is the only territory where he can still assert superiority.
The market has judged him — Fadge got the editorship Alfred coveted — and the Elkanah Settle footnote is how he fights back.
So what looks like comic vanity is also — if you follow it through — a portrait of professional humiliation.
And then Gissing does something extraordinary — he pivots from this broad satirical comedy to something almost gothic without breaking stride.
The fog passage — Marian in that bedroom — is one of the most devastating things in the novel.
And I think it earns its intensity precisely because we've been kept at comic distance for so long.
Gissing writes — and this needs to be heard slowly —

"The thick black fog penetrated every corner of the house. It could be smelt and tasted. Such an atmosphere produces low-spirited languor even in the vigorous and hopeful; to those wasted by suffering it is the very reek of the bottomless pit, poisoning the soul."
The reek of the bottomless pit — Gissing goes full Dante there, and he earns it.
This is the London of the writing poor made into weather, made into something you can smell and taste.
That passage demonstrates what the finest realists understood: atmosphere is not decoration.
It is the externalisation of an inner condition that the prose cannot otherwise reach.
Gissing is right to reach for the Dantean register — Marian's suffering has that quality of the undeserved, the cosmically unjust.
The fog is real too, though — that's the point.
Victorian London's winter fogs were a product of industrial combustion — they killed people.
Marian is not suffering in a metaphor — she is suffering in a specific city at a specific historical moment, in a house she cannot afford to leave.
The fog is both symbol and literal fact — and Gissing keeps both registers alive simultaneously.
But then — and this is the move that I find most astonishing — Gissing follows that with Biffen.
Biffen has just risked his life to rescue his manuscript from a fire — and he responds by turning it into a comic turn.
He imagines the newspaper coverage of his hypothetical death, and he delivers it — in his own words — in a tone of dry deliberation.
"Imagine the gaping wonderment of the coroner's jury!
The Daily Telegraph would have made a leader out of me.

'This poor man was so strangely deluded as to the value of a novel in manuscript, which it appears he had just completed, that he positively sacrificed his life in the endeavour to rescue it from the flames.'"
He's writing his own obituary — and making it funny — because that is all the fame he will ever get.
'At all events, I should have had my day of fame' — Gissing gives him that line, and it lands somewhere between laughter and grief.
Biffen is the figure in the novel I find most sympathetic — and I think most consistently misread.
His comedy is not self-pity dressed up as wit — it is genuine philosophical equanimity in the face of an unforgiving world.
He knows the Saturday Review will sneer — 'the irrepressibly sanguine temperament of authors' — and he pre-empts the sneer by making it himself first.
There is a classical stoicism in that gesture which I find genuinely moving.
I'd frame it differently: Biffen's humour is a survival mechanism in a market that has no use for him.
He can't sell his work, he can't secure patronage, he lives in conditions of near-destitution.
The joke about the Daily Telegraph and the coroner's jury is funny — but it is also an accurate account of how literary culture actually treats its failures.
You only become interesting to a mass readership once you've died for your art — and even then, only as a curiosity.
Comedy shading into pathos, satire sharpening into something close to tragedy — Gissing keeps moving the register on us.
And that restlessness, that refusal to stay in one mode, raises a larger question about how this novel is actually constructed — who is speaking, and from where.
That's what we'll turn to next: the narrative voices of New Grub Street, and the constraints of the form Gissing chose to work in.

segments.title: Narrative Voices and the Constraints of Form

utterances.text: We've been tracing the comedy that Gissing wraps around his literary marketplace — the grotesque farce of Whelpdale, the cold arithmetic of Milvain.
But beneath that satirical surface, the novel is doing something quieter and more devastating — anatomising the inner lives of people who are being destroyed by circumstances they can barely name.
I want to turn now to the question of narrative voice — how Gissing tells us about these characters, and what the form of the novel allows him to show.
What strikes me, returning to the novel now, is the extraordinary economy of Gissing's narration at certain pivotal moments.
He can be expansive — sometimes exhaustingly so — when anatomising Reardon's mental states.
And then he delivers a line of absolute, almost brutal compression.
The marriage of Edwin Reardon and Marian Yule is dispatched in a single sentence.
"Ten weeks thereafter, Miss Yule became Mrs Reardon."
That is everything we are told about the wedding of two people whose destruction will occupy hundreds of subsequent pages.
It is, I think, a masterclass in what the Victorians called the telling detail — or rather, the telling omission.
The happiness is not shown to us because, for Gissing, happiness of this kind is almost beside the point.
Edmund is absolutely right about that compression, and as a performer it stops you cold every time.
You're reading aloud and suddenly you've skipped ten weeks of courtship, the proposal, presumably some tender scene in a drawing room — and you're already in the wreckage.
But what I find equally devastating is when Gissing turns his full attention inward — when he gives Reardon the page to explain himself.
There is a passage where Reardon diagnoses his own collapse with this terrifying, lucid self-knowledge.
"A temperament like mine can't pass through such a violent change of conditions without being greatly affected; I have never since been the man I was before I left England."
And then he turns the knife further.
"I have imagined from time to time that my powers were coming to their ripest; but that was mere delusion. Intellectually, I have fallen back."
The horror of that phrase — "mere delusion" — is that he is not being self-pitying here.
He is being precise.
What I want to press on in that passage is the last line — because Reardon himself names the real cause.
He says his equilibrium might return, that he might recover — and then comes the qualification.
"But the due course of things is troubled by my poverty."
That word — "due" — is doing extraordinary work.
The "due course" of natural development — the proper unfolding of a talent — is what poverty interrupts.
Gissing is not saying Reardon failed because he was weak — he is saying the system extracted from Reardon exactly what it extracts from every worker: the capacity to develop at one's own pace.
The novel's form — that inward, psychologising narration — allows Gissing to show us this from the inside, which is precisely where it does the most damage.
I take Daniel's point about poverty, but I'd resist reducing Reardon entirely to a structural victim.
Gissing is very careful to show us Reardon's self-deceptions alongside his genuine suffering.
There is a passage later in the novel that I find particularly revealing — when Reardon has convinced himself he no longer loves Amy.
"That was the self-deception of misery."
And then Gissing delivers the counter-truth with equal force.
"Love, even passion, was still alive in the depths of his being; the animation with which he sped to his friend as soon as a new hope had risen was the best proof of his feeling."
The narrator here is not sympathising or condemning — he is diagnosing with the cool authority of a physician.
And that, I think, is Gissing's great formal achievement: the omniscient voice that never condescends, never quite forgives, and never fully despairs.
And that quality — the physician's gaze, as Edmund puts it — creates an extraordinary problem for the performer.
Because there are characters in this novel whose inner lives are written with enormous tenderness, and you feel Gissing's affection even through the clinical prose.
Marian Yule is the clearest example.
There is a passage about her feeling for Jasper — about the loneliness that made her vulnerable to him — that is almost unbearably precise.
"Premature, perhaps; why, yes, but one who is starving is not wont to feel reluctance at the suggestion of food."
That metaphor — starvation for emotional sustenance — is not a flourish.
It is the most honest thing the novel says about what isolation does to a person's judgement.
She didn't choose badly — she chose from hunger, which is an entirely different moral category.
Oliver has put his finger on something crucial about Marian, and I want to push it one step further.
Her starvation is not merely emotional — it is the product of a specific material existence.
She is her father's unpaid research assistant, isolated in libraries, denied any ordinary social life.
The novel tells us she had "not known a look of compliment or a word addressed to her emotions" — until Jasper.
That deprivation is structural — it is what her class position and her gender together produce.
And Jasper — perfectly positioned to read her vulnerability — steps into that gap with precisely calibrated attention.
Gissing's narrative voice allows us to see both her feeling and its conditions simultaneously — that is not just psychological realism, it is a kind of critique.
I would only add that the narrative voice Gissing adopts is not, in the end, a polemical instrument — it is a tragic one.
The omniscient narrator in this novel is Olympian precisely because he refuses to assign blame too easily.
We see Reardon's self-deceptions and his genuine love in the same paragraph, without the narrator adjudicating between them.
That is, if I may say so, a deeply classical disposition — closer to the irony of the great Greek tragedians than to any social pamphlet.
A tragic form, then — or perhaps a form that holds tragedy and critique in permanent, unresolved tension.
What we've been circling — the way Gissing's narrative voice refuses to let us look away from what poverty and isolation actually do — brings us, I think, to the largest question the novel asks.
Not just what happens to these particular characters, but what the whole system — the literary marketplace, the class structures sustaining it — leaves behind.
That is what we'll be reckoning with in the final part of our conversation.

segments.title: The System That Devours: Legacy and Reckoning

utterances.text: We've been talking about how Gissing shapes his narrative — the voices, the ironies, the formal constraints that trap his characters.
But I want to end by asking what the novel finally means — what it says about the system itself, and whether anyone escapes it.
What strikes me, returning to the Jasper passages, is how thoroughly Gissing makes him the novel's wicked delight.
He's shameless, and yet somehow you can't quite hate him — because he's the only character who actually sees clearly.

There's a passage where he describes Mrs Boston Wright — this extraordinary woman, shipwrecked, twice married, editor, social queen — and his tone is perfectly pitched between admiration and contempt.
"Mrs Boston Wright cries him up at every opportunity."
That phrase — "cries him up" — does everything: the mutual back-scratching, the literary marketplace as pure performance.
Gissing is laughing, but it's a laugh with sharp edges.
And the laugh sharpens further when you put that passage alongside Jasper's explicit philosophy of literary production.
He isn't concealing anything — he states it baldly, almost proudly.
The line is devastating in its candour:

"a man who has to live by miscellaneous writing couldn't get on without a vast variety of acquaintances. One's own brain would soon run dry; a clever fellow knows how to use the brains of other people."
There it is — the intellectual as parasite, as accumulator of social capital.
Jasper has simply understood what the market demands and stripped away any pretence about inspiration or vocation.
What Gissing shows us is that the literary marketplace doesn't corrupt Jasper — it merely reveals what was always latent in its logic.
I would resist the notion that Jasper is simply the market's creature, however.
Gissing grants him a moment — only a moment, but a genuine one — of something approaching moral seriousness.
In his conversation with Marian, he says — and Gissing is careful to note he is talking into the upper air, a habit when he discusses his own character —

"I don't know that my friendship is worth much. I shall go on as I have begun, and fight for some of the good things of life. But your friendship is valuable. If I am sure of it, I shall be at all events within sight of the better ideals."
"Within sight of the better ideals" — not in possession of them. Not even near them.
That qualification tells you everything about the tragic comedy of Jasper's self-knowledge — he sees his own corruption with perfect clarity, and proceeds anyway.
That is not the market speaking — that is a man choosing.
And yet the choosing is constrained at every turn — look at how Gissing renders Jasper's obligation to Marian in chapter thirty-six.
The engagement he must honour is framed not as a moral duty but as a trap — a self-inflicted doom, in Gissing's own vocabulary.
The narrator tells us starkly:
"he would deliberately be committing the very error always so flagrant to him in the case of other men who had crippled themselves by early marriage with a penniless woman."
Gissing uses the word "crippled" — and he means it economically, materially, with full force.
The system doesn't merely tempt Jasper — it has colonised his interior life so completely that even love registers first as a financial liability.
And the final joke — the culminating punch — comes in chapter thirty-seven.
Someone asks Jasper whom he intends to marry — now that Marian is gone, now that he has his prospects clear before him.
"Amy Reardon."
Two words. His dead friend's widow.
Gissing doesn't editorialise — he simply drops the name into the silence and lets the reader do the work.
It's the most economical condemnation in the novel — and the most perfectly comic, if comedy is the right word for something that cold.
I think it is precisely the right word — Gissing is a comic novelist in the classical sense, which means he takes the measure of human weakness without flinching.
Jasper is not a villain. He is something more uncomfortable — a man of genuine intelligence who has simply decided that scruple is too expensive.
And Reardon, by contrast, pays for his scruples with everything — his marriage, his health, his life.
The novel's deepest question is whether that makes Reardon noble or merely foolish — and Gissing, to his great credit, refuses to adjudicate.
What Gissing does adjudicate — and this is where his radicalism lies — is the system itself.
He does not ask whether individuals are good or bad. He asks what a world looks like when it only rewards the Jaspers.
And the answer — Reardon dead, Marian discarded, Amy pragmatically remarried upward — is not ambiguous.
New Grub Street is one of the great indictments of what capitalism does to the life of the mind — and it has not dated by a single year.
And it is also — I will keep saying this — enormously entertaining.
Gissing's genius is that the indictment comes wrapped in wit, in superb social observation, in characters you cannot stop thinking about.
That is what makes it literature rather than polemic.
I think that's a wonderful place to leave it — the indictment and the delight, held in the same hand.
We've moved through the novel's literary marketplace, its marriages of ambition and exhaustion, its formal ironies, and now its final reckoning with what the system produces and what it destroys.
My warmest thanks to Oliver Trevelyan, whose ear for the prose has been a constant pleasure throughout.
To Sir Edmund Leigh, whose insistence on individual moral accountability has kept us honest at every turn.
And to Dr. Daniel Rosen, whose forensic attention to the structures of power has reminded us what is truly at stake in this novel.
And to you, our listeners — thank you for spending this time with Gissing, with us, and with the inhabitants of New Grub Street.
They deserved better than the world they lived in. The least we can do is read them well.

c31:p98.text:
I should have lived an intelligible life, instead of only trying to live,
      aiming at modes of life beyond my reach. My mistake was that of numberless
      men nowadays. Because I was conscious of brains, I thought that the only
      place for me was London. It’s easy enough to understand this common
      delusion. We form our ideas of London from old literature; we think of
      London as if it were still the one centre of intellectual life; we think
      and talk like Chatterton. But the truth is that intellectual men in our
      day do their best to keep away from London—when once they know the
      place. There are libraries everywhere; papers and magazines reach the
      north of Scotland as soon as they reach Brompton; it’s only on rare
      occasions, for special kinds of work, that one is bound to live in London.
      And as for recreation, why, now that no English theatre exists, what is
      there in London that you can’t enjoy in almost any part of England? At all
      events, a yearly visit of a week would be quite sufficient for all the
      special features of the town. London is only a huge shop, with an hotel on
      the upper storeys. To be sure, if you make it your artistic subject,
      that’s a different thing. But neither you nor I would do that by
      deliberate choice.’
c31:p98.summary: Reardon argues that London is a false magnet for ambitious writers, that intellectual life is available everywhere, and that London ruins artistic men.
c31:p98.best_quote: London is only a huge shop, with an hotel on the upper storeys.

c16:p27.text:
‘Oh, I’ve no doubt of it. If it seemed unlikely, I should have told him so
      before this. To be sure, that’s a point I have often to consider, and once
      or twice my delicacy has asserted itself at the expense of my pocket.
      There was a poor consumptive lad came to me not long ago and wanted Latin
      lessons; talked about going in for the London Matric., on his way to the
      pulpit. I couldn’t stand it. After a lesson or two I told him his cough
      was too bad, and he had no right to study until he got into better health;
      that was better, I think, than saying plainly he had no chance on earth.
      But the food I bought with his money was choking me. Oh yes, Baker will
      make his way right enough. A good, modest fellow.
c16:p27.summary: Biffen recounts his refusal to accept payment from a dying consumptive student preparing for university, choosing kindness over sustenance.
c16:p27.best_quote: After a lesson or two I told him his cough was too bad, and he had no right to study until he got into better health; that was better, I think, than saying plainly he had no chance on earth.

c11:p0.text:
The last volume was written in fourteen days. In this achievement Reardon
      rose almost to heroic pitch, for he had much to contend with beyond the
      mere labour of composition. Scarcely had he begun when a sharp attack of
      lumbago fell upon him; for two or three days it was torture to support
      himself at the desk, and he moved about like a cripple. Upon this ensued
      headaches, sore-throat, general enfeeblement. And before the end of the
      fortnight it was necessary to think of raising another small sum of money;
      he took his watch to the pawnbroker’s (you can imagine that it would not
      stand as security for much), and sold a few more books. All this
      notwithstanding, here was the novel at length finished. When he had
      written ‘The End’ he lay back, closed his eyes, and let time pass in
      blankness for a quarter of an hour.
c11:p0.summary: Reardon completes his novel in two weeks while battling illness, pawning his watch, and selling books to survive financially.
c11:p0.best_quote: The last volume was written in fourteen days. In this achievement Reardon rose almost to heroic pitch, for he had much to contend with beyond the mere labour of composition.

c10:p82.text:
Reardon looked at the gaps left on his shelves. Many of those vanished
      volumes were dear old friends to him; he could have told you where he had
      picked them up and when; to open them recalled a past moment of
      intellectual growth, a mood of hope or despondency, a stage of struggle.
      In most of them his name was written, and there were often pencilled notes
      in the margin. Of course he had chosen from among the most valuable he
      possessed; such a multitude must else have been sold to make this sum of
      two pounds ten. Books are cheap, you know. At need, one can buy a Homer
      for fourpence, a Sophocles for sixpence. It was not rubbish that he had
      accumulated at so small expenditure, but the library of a poor student—battered
      bindings, stained pages, supplanted editions. He loved his books, but
      there was something he loved more, and when Amy glanced at him with eyes
      of sympathy he broke into a cheerful laugh.
c10:p82.summary: Reardon contemplates the gaps left by his sold books, each of which held memories of his intellectual and personal history; yet he chooses his wife's sympathy over his attachment to them.
c10:p82.best_quote: Of course he had chosen from among the most valuable he possessed; such a multitude must else have been sold to make this sum of two pounds ten. Books are cheap, you know.

c11:p77.text:
A doleful Christmas. Week after week went by and Reardon knew that Amy
      must have exhausted the money he had given her. But she made no more
      demands upon him, and necessaries were paid for in the usual way. He
      suffered from a sense of humiliation; sometimes he found it difficult to
      look in his wife’s face.
c11:p77.summary: The Christmas season proves miserable. Weeks pass; Reardon knows Amy's resources are depleted but she does not ask for more. He feels profound humiliation and shame when meeting her gaze.
c11:p77.best_quote: A doleful Christmas. Week after week went by and Reardon knew that Amy must have exhausted the money he had given her. But she made no more demands upon him, and necessaries were paid for in the usual way. He suffered from a sense of humiliation; sometimes he found it difficult to look in his wife's face.

c12:p125.summary: Reardon's anguished reply expresses his complete helplessness and despair—he has no alternative, no way out of his predicament.
c12:p125.best_quote: I wish to Heaven I knew!

c10:p116.text:
They had first met in an amusing way. Not long after the publication of
      his book ‘On Neutral Ground’ Reardon was spending a week at Hastings. A
      rainy day drove him to the circulating library, and as he was looking
      along the shelves for something readable a voice near at hand asked the
      attendant if he had anything ‘by Edwin Reardon.’ The novelist turned in
      astonishment; that any casual mortal should inquire for his books seemed
      incredible. Of course there was nothing by that author in the library, and
      he who had asked the question walked out again. On the morrow Reardon
      encountered this same man at a lonely part of the shore; he looked at him,
      and spoke a word or two of common civility; they got into conversation,
      with the result that Edwin told the story of yesterday. The stranger
      introduced himself as Harold Biffen, an author in a small way, and a
      teacher whenever he could get pupils; an abusive review had interested him
      in Reardon’s novels, but as yet he knew nothing of them but the names.
c10:p116.summary: The narrative reveals how Reardon and Biffen first met at Hastings: Biffen inquired for Reardon's books at a circulating library, then they encountered each other by chance the next day at the shore, and discovered their shared literary interests.
c10:p116.best_quote: a voice near at hand asked the attendant if he had anything 'by Edwin Reardon.' The novelist turned in astonishment; that any casual mortal should inquire for his books seemed incredible

c12:p100.text:
‘You don’t know what he’s doing? The fellow has set up as a “literary
      adviser.” He has an advertisement in The Study every week. “To Young
      Authors and Literary Aspirants”—something of the kind. “Advice given
      on choice of subjects, MSS. read, corrected, and recommended to
      publishers. Moderate terms.” A fact! And what’s more, he made six guineas
      in the first fortnight; so he says, at all events. Now that’s one of the
      finest jokes I ever heard. A man who can’t get anyone to publish his own
      books makes a living by telling other people how to write!’
c12:p100.summary: Jasper recounts that Whelpdale has set up as a 'literary adviser,' advertising in The Study, charging modest fees to give advice on writing and recommend manuscripts to publishers; he reportedly made six guineas in his first fortnight.
c12:p100.best_quote: A man who can't get anyone to publish his own books makes a living by telling other people how to write!

c33:p49.text:
‘No, I am perfectly serious. Let me explain my principle. I would have the
      paper address itself to the quarter-educated; that is to say, the great
      new generation that is being turned out by the Board schools, the young
      men and women who can just read, but are incapable of sustained attention.
      People of this kind want something to occupy them in trains and on ‘buses
      and trams. As a rule they care for no newspapers except the Sunday ones;
      what they want is the lightest and frothiest of chit-chatty information—bits
      of stories, bits of description, bits of scandal, bits of jokes, bits of
      statistics, bits of foolery. Am I not right? Everything must be very
      short, two inches at the utmost; their attention can’t sustain itself
      beyond two inches. Even chat is too solid for them: they want chit-chat.’
c33:p49.summary: Whelpdale explains his philosophy: the magazine should target the quarter-educated mass produced by Board schools—young people who can barely read and cannot sustain attention. They want brief fragments of information while travelling, not substantial articles. Everything must be extremely short, as their concentration cannot exceed two inches of text.
c33:p49.best_quote: People of this kind want something to occupy them in trains and on 'buses and trams. As a rule they care for no newspapers except the Sunday ones; what they want is the lightest and frothiest of chit-chatty information—bits of stories, bits of description, bits of scandal, bits of jokes, bits of statistics, bits of foolery.

c21:p174.text:
She did not think it probable that she herself would benefit directly by
      John Yule’s will. There was no certainty that even her father would, for
      he and his brother had never been on cordial terms. But on the whole it
      seemed likely that he would inherit money enough to free him from the toil
      of writing for periodicals. He himself anticipated that. What else could
      be the meaning of those words in which (and it was before the arrival of
      the news) he had warned her against ‘people who made connections only with
      self-interest in view?’ This threw a sudden light upon her father’s
      attitude towards Jasper Milvain. Evidently he thought that Jasper regarded
      her as a possible heiress, sooner or later. That suspicion was rankling in
      his mind; doubtless it intensified the prejudice which originated in
      literary animosity.
c21:p174.summary: Marian understands that her father believes Jasper Milvain pursues her for her potential inheritance, and this explains his intensified prejudice against the young man.
c21:p174.best_quote: This threw a sudden light upon her father's attitude towards Jasper Milvain. Evidently he thought that Jasper regarded her as a possible heiress, sooner or later. That suspicion was rankling in his mind; doubtless it intensified the prejudice which originated in literary animosity

c36:p119.text:
‘I know now,’ she said, ‘how foolish it is when they talk of love being
      unselfish. In what can there be more selfishness? I feel as if I could
      hold you to your promise at any cost, though you have made me understand
      that you regard our engagement as your great misfortune. I have felt it
      for weeks—oh, for months! But I couldn’t say a word that would seem
      to invite such misery as this. You don’t love me, Jasper, and that’s an
      end of everything.
c36:p119.summary: Marian achieves tragic clarity: she recognizes that love is fundamentally selfish, that Jasper has never truly loved her, and she resolves to end the engagement despite her desires.
c36:p119.best_quote: I know now how foolish it is when they talk of love being unselfish. In what can there be more selfishness? I feel as if I could hold you to your promise at any cost, though you have made me understand that you regard our engagement as your great misfortune. You don't love me, Jasper, and that's an end of everything.

c9:p2.text:
The latter alternative was often enough before him. He seldom slept for
      more than two or three consecutive hours in the night, and the time of
      wakefulness was often terrible. The various sounds which marked the stages
      from midnight to dawn had grown miserably familiar to him; worst torture
      to his mind was the chiming and striking of clocks. Two of these were in
      general audible, that of Marylebone parish church, and that of the
      adjoining workhouse; the latter always sounded several minutes after its
      ecclesiastical neighbour, and with a difference of note which seemed to
      Reardon very appropriate—a thin, querulous voice, reminding one of
      the community it represented. After lying awake for awhile he would hear
      quarters sounding; if they ceased before the fourth he was glad, for he
      feared to know what time it was. If the hour was complete, he waited
      anxiously for its number. Two, three, even four, were grateful; there was
      still a long time before he need rise and face the dreaded task, the
      horrible four blank slips of paper that had to be filled ere he might
      sleep again. But such restfulness was only for a moment; no sooner had the
      workhouse bell become silent than he began to toil in his weary
      imagination, or else, incapable of that, to vision fearful hazards of the
      future. The soft breathing of Amy at his side, the contact of her warm
      limbs, often filled him with intolerable dread. Even now he did not
      believe that Amy loved him with the old love, and the suspicion was like a
      cold weight at his heart that to retain even her wifely sympathy, her
      wedded tenderness, he must achieve the impossible.
c9:p2.summary: Reardon suffers from chronic insomnia tormented by the chiming of church and workhouse clocks; the dread of blank pages and fear of Amy's waning love intensify his mental anguish.
c9:p2.best_quote: The soft breathing of Amy at his side, the contact of her warm limbs, often filled him with intolerable dread. Even now he did not believe that Amy loved him with the old love, and the suspicion was like a cold weight at his heart that to retain even her wifely sympathy, her wedded tenderness, he must achieve the impossible.

c13:p51.text:
She could not trust herself to converse longer. A resentment such as her
      father had never yet excited in her—such, indeed, as she had seldom,
      if ever, conceived—threatened to force utterance for itself in words
      which would change the current of her whole life. She saw her father in
      his worst aspect, and her heart was shaken by an unnatural revolt from
      him. Let his assurance of what he reported be ever so firm, what right had
      he to make this use of it? His behaviour was spiteful. Suppose he
      entertained suspicions which seemed to make it his duty to warn her
      against Milvain, this was not the way to go about it. A father actuated by
      simple motives of affection would never speak and look thus.
c13:p51.summary: Unable to continue, Marian retreats, fearing she will say words that would irreversibly change her life. She recognizes her father's spitefulness and realizes that a genuinely loving father would never employ such cruel methods, no matter his concerns.
c13:p51.best_quote: She saw her father in his worst aspect, and her heart was shaken by an unnatural revolt from him.

c14:p137.text:
‘Dull, by no means. But sage and sober and reticent—and exactly what
      I like in my friend, because it contrasts with my own habits. All the
      better that merriment lies below it. Goodnight, Miss Yule.’
c14:p137.summary: Jasper affirms that Marian is far from dull, and that her serious, reserved nature contrasts pleasantly with his own ebullience, especially now that he sees she has hidden depths of humour.
c14:p137.best_quote: Dull, by no means. But sage and sober and reticent—and exactly what I like in my friend, because it contrasts with my own habits. All the better that merriment lies below it.

c9:p10.text:
For months he had been living in this way; endless circling, perpetual
      beginning, followed by frustration. A sign of exhaustion, it of course
      made exhaustion more complete. At times he was on the border-land of
      imbecility; his mind looked into a cloudy chaos, a shapeless whirl of
      nothings. He talked aloud to himself, not knowing that he did so. Little
      phrases which indicated dolorously the subject of his preoccupation often
      escaped him in the street: ‘What could I make of that, now?’ ‘Well,
      suppose I made him—?’ ‘But no, that wouldn’t do,’ and so on. It had
      happened that he caught the eye of some one passing fixed in surprise upon
      him; so young a man to be talking to himself in evident distress!
c9:p10.summary: Months of endless circling and perpetual false starts have pushed Reardon toward mental collapse; he talks aloud in distress on the streets, his mind a shapeless chaos, not knowing who observes him.
c9:p10.best_quote: At times he was on the border-land of imbecility; his mind looked into a cloudy chaos, a shapeless whirl of nothings. He talked aloud to himself, not knowing that he did so. Little phrases which indicated dolorously the subject of his preoccupation often escaped him in the street: 'What could I make of that, now?' 'Well, suppose I made him—?' 'But no, that wouldn't do,' and so on.

c16:p97.text:
‘She writes—that she has met an old lover—in Birmingham—that
      it was with him she had quarrelled-not with her father at all—that
      she ran away to annoy him and frighten him—that she has made it up
      again, and they’re going to be married!’
c16:p97.summary: Whelpdale reveals that his fiancée's letter explains she has reunited with an old lover in Birmingham and will marry him instead.
c16:p97.best_quote: She writes—that she has met an old lover—in Birmingham—that it was with him she had quarrelled-not with her father at all—that she ran away to annoy him and frighten him—that she has made it up again, and they're going to be married!

c16:p92.text:
He tore open the envelope. In delicacy Reardon and Biffen averted their
      eyes. There was silence for a minute, then a strange ejaculation from
      Whelpdale caused his friends to look up at him. He had gone pale, and was
      frowning at the sheet of paper which trembled in his hand.
c16:p92.summary: Whelpdale turns pale and trembles while reading the letter, his joy transformed instantly into shock and dismay.
c16:p92.best_quote: He had gone pale, and was frowning at the sheet of paper which trembled in his hand.

c2:p77.text:
‘Civilisation!’ exclaimed John, scornfully. ‘What do you mean by
      civilisation? Do you call it civilising men to make them weak, flabby
      creatures, with ruined eyes and dyspeptic stomachs? Who is it that reads
      most of the stuff that’s poured out daily by the ton from the
      printing-press? Just the men and women who ought to spend their leisure
      hours in open-air exercise; the people who earn their bread by sedentary
      pursuits, and who need to live as soon as they are free from the desk or
      the counter, not to moon over small print. Your Board schools, your
      popular press, your spread of education! Machinery for ruining the
      country, that’s what I call it.’
c2:p77.summary: John launches into a scornful denunciation of civilization as weakening people through reading and sedentary pursuits; he attacks Board schools, popular press, and education as ruining England by making people pale, weak, and dyspeptic instead of promoting physical vigor and outdoor life.
c2:p77.best_quote: Your Board schools, your popular press, your spread of education! Machinery for ruining the country, that's what I call it.

c3:p121.text:
‘... The evil of the time is the multiplication of ephemerides. Hence a
      demand for essays, descriptive articles, fragments of criticism, out of
      all proportion to the supply of even tolerable work. The men who have an
      aptitude for turning out this kind of thing in vast quantities are
      enlisted by every new periodical, with the result that their productions
      are ultimately watered down into worthlessness.... Well now, there’s
      Fadge. Years ago some of Fadge’s work was not without a certain—a
      certain conditional promise of—of comparative merit; but now his
      writing, in my opinion, is altogether beneath consideration; how Rackett
      could be so benighted as to give him The Study—especially after a
      man like Henry Hawkridge—passes my comprehension. Did you read a
      paper of his, a few months back, in The Wayside, a preposterous
      rehabilitation of Elkanah Settle? Ha! Ha! That’s what such men are driven
      to. Elkanah Settle! And he hadn’t even a competent acquaintance with his
      paltry subject. Will you credit that he twice or thrice referred to
      Settle’s reply to “Absalom and Achitophel” by the title of “Absalom
      Transposed,” when every schoolgirl knows that the thing was called
      “Achitophel Transposed”! This was monstrous enough, but there was
      something still more contemptible. He positively, I assure you, attributed
      the play of “Epsom Wells” to Crowne! I should have presumed that every
      student of even the most trivial primer of literature was aware that
      “Epsom Wells” was written by Shadwell.... Now, if one were to take
      Shadwell for the subject of a paper, one might very well show how unjustly
      his name has fallen into contempt. It has often occurred to me to do this.
      “But Shadwell never deviates into sense.” The sneer, in my opinion, is
      entirely unmerited. For my own part, I put Shadwell very high among the
      dramatists of his time, and I think I could show that his absolute worth
      is by no means inconsiderable. Shadwell has distinct vigour of dramatic
      conception; his dialogue....’
c3:p121.summary: Alfred launches into a passionate critique of modern literary journalism: too many periodicals demand mediocre content; Fadge exemplifies declining standards through scholarly errors; yet Shadwell deserves reconsideration as a neglected dramatist.
c3:p121.best_quote: The evil of the time is the multiplication of ephemerides. Hence a demand for essays, descriptive articles, fragments of criticism, out of all proportion to the supply of even tolerable work.

c30:p150.text:
The thick black fog penetrated every corner of the house. It could be
      smelt and tasted. Such an atmosphere produces low-spirited languor even in
      the vigorous and hopeful; to those wasted by suffering it is the very reek
      of the bottomless pit, poisoning the soul. Her face colourless as the
      pillow, Marian lay neither sleeping nor awake, in blank extremity of woe;
      tears now and then ran down her cheeks, and at times her body was shaken
      with a throe such as might result from anguish of the torture chamber.
c30:p150.summary: The narrator evokes the oppressive London fog as a physical manifestation of Marian's emotional anguish; it is almost Dantean in its suggestion of hellish suffering.
c30:p150.best_quote: The thick black fog penetrated every corner of the house. It could be smelt and tasted. Such an atmosphere produces low-spirited languor even in the vigorous and hopeful; to those wasted by suffering it is the very reek of the bottomless pit, poisoning the soul

c31:p91.text:
‘Thinking of my fiery adventure,’ he said, in his tone of dry
      deliberation, ‘I find it vastly amusing to picture you as a witness at the
      inquest if I had been choked and consumed. No doubt it would have been
      made known that I rushed upstairs to save some particular piece of
      property—several people heard me say so—and you alone would be
      able to conjecture what this was. Imagine the gaping wonderment of the
      coroner’s jury! The Daily Telegraph would have made a leader out of me.
      “This poor man was so strangely deluded as to the value of a novel in
      manuscript, which it appears he had just completed, that he positively
      sacrificed his life in the endeavour to rescue it from the flames.” And
      the Saturday would have had a column of sneering jocosity on the
      irrepressibly sanguine temperament of authors. At all events, I should
      have had my day of fame.’
c31:p91.summary: Biffen jokes that he would have received posthumous literary fame if the fire had killed him while saving his manuscript.
c31:p91.best_quote: Imagine the gaping wonderment of the coroner's jury! The Daily Telegraph would have made a leader out of me. "This poor man was so strangely deluded as to the value of a novel in manuscript, which it appears he had just completed, that he positively sacrificed his life in the endeavour to rescue it from the flames."

c5:p43.text: Ten weeks thereafter, Miss Yule became Mrs Reardon.
c5:p43.summary: Marian and Edwin marry ten weeks after their first meeting.
c5:p43.best_quote: Ten weeks thereafter, Miss Yule became Mrs Reardon.

c6:p93.text:
‘That half-year abroad, and the extraordinary shock of happiness which
      followed at once upon it, have disturbed the balance of my nature. It was
      adjusted to circumstances of hardship, privation, struggle. A temperament
      like mine can’t pass through such a violent change of conditions without
      being greatly affected; I have never since been the man I was before I
      left England. The stage I had then reached was the result of a slow and
      elaborate building up; I could look back and see the processes by which I
      had grown from the boy who was a mere bookworm to the man who had all but
      succeeded as a novelist. It was a perfectly natural, sober development.
      But in the last two years and a half I can distinguish no order. In living
      through it, I have imagined from time to time that my powers were coming
      to their ripest; but that was mere delusion. Intellectually, I have fallen
      back. The probability is that this wouldn’t matter, if only I could live
      on in peace of mind; I should recover my equilibrium, and perhaps once
      more understand myself. But the due course of things is troubled by my
      poverty.’
c6:p93.summary: Reardon analyzes how his sojourn abroad and the subsequent shock of happiness with Amy disrupted his previously balanced development, leading to intellectual decline and mental paralysis aggravated by financial desperation; he contrasts his formerly natural development with his current disordered state.
c6:p93.best_quote: A temperament like mine can't pass through such a violent change of conditions without being greatly affected; I have never since been the man I was before I left England... I have imagined from time to time that my powers were coming to their ripest; but that was mere delusion. Intellectually, I have fallen back... But the due course of things is troubled by my poverty.

c25:p59.text:
In truth, there needed little persuasion. Perverseness, one of the forms
      or issues of self-pity, made him strive against his desire, and caused him
      to adopt a tone of acerbity in excess of what he felt; but already he had
      made up his mind to see Amy. Even if this excuse had not presented itself
      he must very soon have yielded to the longing for a sight of his wife’s
      face which day by day increased among all the conflicting passions of
      which he was the victim. A month or two ago, when the summer sunshine made
      his confinement to the streets a daily torture, he convinced himself that
      there remained in him no trace of his love for Amy; there were moments
      when he thought of her with repugnance, as a cold, selfish woman, who had
      feigned affection when it seemed her interest to do so, but brutally
      declared her true self when there was no longer anything to be hoped from
      him. That was the self-deception of misery. Love, even passion, was still
      alive in the depths of his being; the animation with which he sped to his
      friend as soon as a new hope had risen was the best proof of his feeling.
c25:p59.summary: Gissing explains that though Reardon's perverseness made him resist his desire to see Amy, he has already decided to do so; his love for her has never truly died despite months of self-convinced conviction to the contrary, and his eagerness reveals the passionate core beneath his bitterness.
c25:p59.best_quote: Love, even passion, was still alive in the depths of his being; the animation with which he sped to his friend as soon as a new hope had risen was the best proof of his feeling

c14:p149.text:
Alone in her room she sat down only to think of Jasper Milvain, and
      extract from the memory of his words, his looks, new sustenance for her
      hungry heart. Jasper was the first man who had ever evinced a man’s
      interest in her. Until she met him she had not known a look of compliment
      or a word addressed to her emotions. He was as far as possible from
      representing the lover of her imagination, but from the day of that long
      talk in the fields near Wattleborough the thought of him had supplanted
      dreams. On that day she said to herself: I could love him if he cared to
      seek my love. Premature, perhaps; why, yes, but one who is starving is not
      wont to feel reluctance at the suggestion of food. The first man who had
      approached her with display of feeling and energy and youthful
      self-confidence; handsome too, it seemed to her. Her womanhood went
      eagerly to meet him.
c14:p149.summary: Marian recalls that Jasper was the first man to show romantic interest in her, the first to offer her emotional and intellectual engagement. Despite his flaws, she was drawn to his energy and self-confidence. Her loneliness made her eager to love.
c14:p149.best_quote: Premature, perhaps; why, yes, but one who is starving is not wont to feel reluctance at the suggestion of food.

c12:p84.text:
‘Nonsense!—Miss Wilkes, of course. Well, she married this fellow
      Jedwood, and there was a great row about something or other between him
      and her publishers. Mrs Boston Wright told me all about it. An astonishing
      woman that; a cyclopaedia of the day’s small talk. I’m quite a favourite
      with her; she’s promised to help the girls all she can. Well, but I was
      talking about Jedwood. Why not offer him this book of yours? He’s eager to
      get hold of the new writers. Advertises hugely; he has the whole back page
      of The Study about every other week. I suppose Miss Wilkes’s profits are
      paying for it. He has just given Markland two hundred pounds for a paltry
      little tale that would scarcely swell out to a volume. Markland told me
      himself. You know that I’ve scraped an acquaintance with him? Oh! I
      suppose I haven’t seen you since then. He’s a dwarfish fellow with only
      one eye. Mrs Boston Wright cries him up at every opportunity.’
c12:p84.summary: Jasper recounts the extraordinary life story of Mrs Boston Wright—born in a colonial location, shipwrecked, newspaper correspondent, farmer, twice married, widow—now editor of The English Girl and a central figure in London's literary society; she is nearly fifty but appears much younger; Jasper has cultivated her as a useful connection and promises to introduce Reardon and Amy.
c12:p84.best_quote: Mrs Boston Wright cries him up at every opportunity.

c12:p96.text:
‘The simplest thing in the world. At present it’s a large part of my
      business to make acquaintances. Why, look you; a man who has to live by
      miscellaneous writing couldn’t get on without a vast variety of
      acquaintances. One’s own brain would soon run dry; a clever fellow knows
      how to use the brains of other people.’
c12:p96.summary: Jasper explains that his business as a writer requires cultivating broad acquaintances because miscellaneous writing exhausts one's own ideas; a clever man learns to leverage other people's ideas and connections rather than rely solely on his own talent.
c12:p96.best_quote: a man who has to live by miscellaneous writing couldn't get on without a vast variety of acquaintances. One's own brain would soon run dry; a clever fellow knows how to use the brains of other people.

c14:p129.text:
‘I don’t know that my friendship is worth much,’ Jasper continued, talking
      into the upper air, a habit of his when he discussed his own character. ‘I
      shall go on as I have begun, and fight for some of the good things of
      life. But your friendship is valuable. If I am sure of it, I shall be at
      all events within sight of the better ideals.’
c14:p129.summary: Jasper acknowledges his moral compromises but argues that Marian's friendship would anchor him to better ideals.
c14:p129.best_quote: I don't know that my friendship is worth much. I shall go on as I have begun, and fight for some of the good things of life. But your friendship is valuable. If I am sure of it, I shall be at all events within sight of the better ideals.

c36:p1.text:
A part of that impression was due to the engagement which he must now
      fulfil. He had pledged his word to ask Marian to marry him without further
      delay. To shuffle out of this duty would make him too ignoble even in his
      own eyes. Its discharge meant, as he had expressed it, that he was
      ‘doomed’; he would deliberately be committing the very error always so
      flagrant to him in the case of other men who had crippled themselves by
      early marriage with a penniless woman. But events had enmeshed him;
      circumstances had proved fatal. Because, in his salad days, he dallied
      with a girl who had indeed many charms, step by step he had come to the
      necessity of sacrificing his prospects to that raw attachment. And, to
      make it more irritating, this happened just when the way began to be much
      clearer before him.
c36:p1.summary: Jasper is bound by his pledge to propose to Marian, viewing it as a self-inflicted doom that contradicts his own principles and comes at precisely the moment his prospects brighten.
c36:p1.best_quote: he would deliberately be committing the very error always so flagrant to him in the case of other men who had crippled themselves by early marriage with a penniless woman

c37:p33.summary: Jasper reveals that he intends to marry Amy Reardon, Edwin Reardon's widow.
